When a single-page website is best (Andrés Max)

I remember when a big concern in web design was "the fold." The idea was that it was important to decide what goes in the area of the page that will be seen initially without scrolling (it was an inexact science, of course, with many possible screen and window sizes and such). This would be the most important stuff and the assumption was that most users wouldn't scroll down, hence you had to consider well what was exiled to the "below the fold" wasteland.

For various reasons users and designers have decided that scrolling is awesome, and these super-long one-page sites are all the rage. But I've just found a Nielsen Norman Group posting from 2015 arguing in favor of keeping the fold in mind: http://www.nngroup.com/articles/page-fold-manifesto/

Rioting inmates at Attica Correctional Facility voice their demands during a negotiating session with New York's prison Commissioner on Sept. 10, 1971.

The Attica Prison riot occurred at the Attica Correctional Facility in Attica, New York, United States in 1971. This riot is one of the most famous and important riots during the Prisoners' Rights Movement. The riot was based upon prisoners' demands for political rights and better living conditions. On September 9, 1971, two weeks after the killing of George Jackson at San Quentin, about 1,000 of the Attica prison's approximately 2,200 inmates rioted and seized control of the prison, taking 42 staff hostage.

During the following four days of negotiations, authorities agreed to 28 of the prisoners' demands, but would not agree to demands for complete amnesty from criminal prosecution for the prison takeover or for the removal of Attica's superintendent. By the order of state Governor Nelson Rockefeller, state police took back control of the prison. When the uprising was over, at least 43 people were dead, including ten correctional officers and civilian employees, and 33 inmates.
